subcategory: Responsible AI, Human Rights and Safety
oneSentence: The gap between people who can reliably use digital tools and services and those who cannot, because of access, cost, skills, language, design or safety barriers.
plainExplanation:
A digital divide is an unequal ability to use digital technology in real life. The gap can start with basic access: no device, weak electricity, slow mobile signal, expensive data, or no broadband. It can also continue after connection exists, if people cannot afford enough data, do not have the needed skills, face language barriers, or use services that are not accessible.

What goes in are people with different circumstances. These include income, age, disability, location, education, gender, language, legal status and safety risks. Then digital systems are introduced: online forms, mobile apps, AI tools, remote learning, digital payments or information services.

What happens is that some people can use these systems easily, while others are partly excluded or pushed into harder, slower or more risky paths. A service may assume constant internet, a modern smartphone, literacy in one language, or the confidence to share data online. If those assumptions are wrong, the gap widens.

What comes out is unequal participation and unequal outcomes. Some people get information, services, jobs or a voice in decision-making sooner and more safely. Others may be missed, misrepresented or forced to depend on intermediaries. In AI work, this matters because systems built for the connected population may perform poorly or unfairly for everyone else.

The digital divide is often confused with the AI divide. They overlap, but they are not the same. The digital divide is broader: it includes ordinary internet and device access, digital skills and safe use. The AI divide focuses more specifically on who can build, use or benefit from AI systems.

everydayAnalogy.title: One survey, many ways to get left out
everydayAnalogy.story: A city team asks residents to report local problems through an online survey. Lina answers on her phone in a few minutes because she has data, the form loads quickly, and it appears in her language. Samuel has an older phone and limited data, so the map on the page never fully opens. Amina can get online at a library, but the survey is not screen-reader friendly, so she cannot complete it independently. By the end, the team receives many reports from some neighbourhoods and almost none from others, even though the problems exist in all of them.

mapping.analogyElement: Residents with different phones, data plans and needs
mapping.aiElement: People facing different levels of digital access, affordability and accessibility

mapping.analogyElement: A survey that assumes a fast connection and one design style
mapping.aiElement: Digital services built with hidden assumptions about users
Unequal participation that produces incomplete or biased outcomes

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A survey is one short task, but the digital divide affects many parts of life over time, such as schooling, work, health information and civic participation. The analogy also focuses on using a service, while the real issue includes creating technology, shaping standards, and deciding whose needs are considered in the first place.

visual.title: How a digital divide turns into unequal outcomes
visual.learningObjective: Show how barriers in access, affordability, skills, language and design can lead to lower participation and less fair outcomes.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four stages. Stage 1 lists people with different starting conditions. Stage 2 shows common barriers. Stage 3 shows different levels of digital participation. Stage 4 shows practical outcomes such as who receives information, services or influence. Read from left to right to see how small barriers accumulate.

steps.label: Different starting points
steps.explanation: People begin with different devices, connections, incomes, skills, languages and accessibility needs.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a column of simple person icons with small labels: strong connection, weak signal, shared phone, low literacy, screen reader user, rural area.

steps.label: Barriers appear
steps.explanation: A service may require constant internet, a newer device, paid data, one language or a design some users cannot access.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second column of barrier cards between people and the service: cost, coverage, device limits, skills, language, inaccessible design, safety concerns.

steps.label: Participation splits
steps.explanation: Some users complete the task easily. Others abandon it, need help, or never start.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw arrows from barriers to three outcomes: completed independently, completed with difficulty, not completed. Make arrow thickness vary to show unequal numbers.

steps.label: Outcomes become unequal
steps.explanation: The final results under-represent some groups, which can distort decisions and make services less fair.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final column with icons for information received, service access, representation in data and decision quality; fade or reduce some icons for excluded groups.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each barrier to highlight which users it affects and which outcome changes.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains a chain of cause and effect. First, people start from different situations: some have strong internet, some weak signal, some share a phone, some need assistive technology, and some have limited digital skills or different languages. Second, barriers in the service appear, such as high data cost, poor coverage, old-device incompatibility, inaccessible design or safety concerns. Third, participation splits: some complete the task easily, some complete it with difficulty, and some cannot complete it. Fourth, outcomes become unequal because the final information and services reflect the people who could participate most easily.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-column chart replaces animation. Arrows connect starting conditions to barriers, barriers to participation levels, and participation levels to outcomes, with colour and labels showing where exclusion increases.

workedExample.scenario: A public health team offers vaccine appointment booking through a mobile website in one city and nearby rural districts.
workedExample.input: 10,000 adults are invited by text message. Surveys later show: 7,000 have a smartphone with regular data, 2,000 have a basic phone or an older smartphone, and 1,000 share a device or have weak network coverage.
process: The booking site is designed for smartphones, uses a map that needs strong data, and is available only in two languages.
Of the 7,000 with regular data, 5,600 complete a booking. Of the 2,000 with older or basic devices, 700 complete it. Of the 1,000 sharing devices or facing weak coverage, 150 complete it.
The team sees high booking rates in connected areas and low rates elsewhere, even though need is similar across districts.
They add a lighter web page, more languages, a phone hotline and in-person booking support, then completion rises in the previously excluded groups.
workedExample.result: The first version measured digital access as much as health demand. After the service design changed, participation became more representative and fairer.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: After a disaster, a UN team uses satellite imagery and digital reports to help identify affected areas and prioritise follow-up assessments.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: If the analysis relies mainly on app reports or online submissions, communities with weak connectivity, low phone access or inaccessible reporting channels may appear less affected than they really are. Recognising the digital divide helps teams combine remote analysis with offline outreach and human verification.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not assume lack of digital reports means lack of need, and do not put personal, protection-sensitive or location-sensitive information into an unapproved public AI service.

whyItMatters: The digital divide changes who is seen, heard and served. If a programme, policy or AI system assumes everyone has stable internet, a private device, enough data, the right language and the skills to use digital tools safely, decisions will favour some groups over others. That can produce unfair service delivery, misleading data, weaker consultation and higher risk for people already facing disadvantage. For non-specialists, the key point is practical: before relying on digital or AI systems, ask who can realistically use them, who cannot, and what non-digital or supported alternatives are needed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It only means some people do not have internet access.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Access matters, but the gap is wider than connection alone. People may be technically online and still be excluded by data cost, device limits, disability barriers, low digital skills, language mismatch, harassment risks or lack of trust.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once most people have smartphones, the problem is basically solved.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A phone does not guarantee meaningful use. An older device, expensive data, poor battery charging, unsafe shared access, inaccessible app design or forms that require high literacy can still block participation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: This is a technology issue, not a human rights or fairness issue.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Digital access shapes access to information, services, participation and remedy. When important systems move online, unequal digital access can reinforce discrimination or exclusion, so the issue affects fairness, inclusion and accountability.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Some people can use digital services easily, and some cannot. The difference comes from things like connection, cost, devices, skills, language, accessibility and safety.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: The digital divide refers to uneven capacity to access, afford, use and benefit from digital technologies and digital public or private services. It includes first-level access gaps such as electricity, network coverage, devices and bandwidth; second-level gaps such as digital literacy, language support, accessibility and trust; and outcome gaps, meaning differences in who can convert digital access into real social, economic or civic benefits. In AI contexts, the divide matters at several stages: whose data is captured, who can interact with AI-enabled services, who receives the benefits, and whose needs are under-represented in design, evaluation and oversight. It is related to inclusion and accessibility, but it is not identical to either one. Accessibility focuses on whether systems work for people with disabilities. Inclusion is broader and may include social participation beyond technology. The digital divide also differs from the AI divide, which more specifically concerns unequal access to AI capabilities, infrastructure, expertise and benefits.

keyTakeaway: If a digital service works well only for the already connected, it can widen existing inequalities instead of reducing them.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows a digital divide rather than only a technical glitch?
options: A website is offline for one hour because of server maintenance.
A job application is only online, uses high data, and does not work with screen readers, so many qualified people cannot apply.
A team chooses a blue design theme that some users dislike.
One person forgets their password and asks for a reset.
quickCheck.explanation: The digital divide is about unequal ability to access and use digital systems in real conditions. The second option combines affordability, accessibility and design barriers that exclude part of the population, which is the core issue.
